title: Variant-Aware CRISPR Diagnostics Under Pathogen Evolution: From Computational Design to Clinical Translation and Adaptive Updating
content: CRISPR-based diagnostics (CRISPR-Dx) have emerged as programmable platforms for rapid nucleic acid detection, but their reliable translation is challenged by continuous pathogen genomic evolution. Sequence variation can alter target conservation, primer compatibility, guide activity, and variant discrimination, making reference-based design increasingly inadequate. This review examines CRISPR-Dx as a computationally informed, multistage design problem in which pathogen diversity, target selection, primer-guide compatibility, functional prediction, evolutionary objectives, and downstream diagnostic constraints are interconnected. It synthesizes approaches spanning whole-genome and population-aware target discovery, integrated primer-guide design, machine-learning-based guide prediction, computational benchmarking, variant-resilient and discriminatory targeting, guide engineering, and model-directed sequence generation. Particular emphasis is placed on separating computational evidence from experimental, analytical, clinical, and deployment evidence, because improvements in upstream prediction do not necessarily translate proportionally into diagnostic performance. Resilience, which seeks sustained detection across evolving pathogen populations, is distinguished from discrimination, which exploits defined sequence differences for variant identification. Building on these observations, an adaptive CRISPR-Dx framework is proposed that links surveillance, design, testing, deployment, and updating. The major unresolved challenge is establishing this cycle prospectively, with explicit validation thresholds, uncertainty management, and regulatory control, under real-world pathogen evolution.
